label: LIVE CLAUDE

messages_in.content:
TASK
Propose 3 distinct stress scenarios over a horizon of at most 30 days in which the book below loses at least $5,000,000 (a loss means negative total P&L).
Driver family: cold_snap
Season: winter


INPUTS
Context (units: prices $/MWh, gas $/MMBtu, power MW, time days):

  },

   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows below c0",
   "position": "P2",

  },
  {
   "channel": "dart",
   "gains_when": "real-time clears below day-ahead",
   "loses_when": "real-time clears above day-ahead (real-time spikes)",
   "position": "P3",
   "what": "Receives (day-ahead minus real-time) at WEST off-peak on 50 MW (8 h, 24 h on weekends and holidays)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "gas",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak price rises relative to gas",
   "loses_when": "scenario losses are measured against the unshocked path (the premium cancels), so P4 loses only when its payoff falls BELOW the unshocked payoff, i.e. when gas rises more than power; it can never lose more than that base payoff",
   "position": "P4",
   "what": "Long heat-rate call on 50 MW, on-peak: pays max(WEST on-peak - 8 x gas - 3, 0) minus a premium of 8.29 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  },
  {
   "channel": "zone_volume",
   "gains_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread narrows",
   "loses_when": "the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens; the loss also grows with load above normal",
   "position": "P5",

  },
  {
   "channel": "tail",
   "gains_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average stays below K6",
   "loses_when": "the WEST on-peak daily average exceeds K6 (price spikes)",
   "position": "P6",
   "what": "Short call on 25 MW of the WEST on-peak daily average, strike K6 = 149.31 $/MWh, premium received 0.53 $/MWh (fair value on the fit sample)"
  }
 ],
 "book_summary": "P1 (when its size is positive) and P4 are LONG WEST power, so higher WEST prices make them GAIN (a negative P1 size is a SHORT swap that loses when WEST rises); higher gas lowers P4. CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.

scenario.narrative: A prolonged 25-day cold spell lifts the daily peak load 12% above a typical winter day (ratio 1.12, below the historical winter maximum of 1.196). Gas rises 80% at Henry Hub. Upstate generation can serve WEST, but the New York City pocket is constrained, so N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $100/MWh, similar to the gap between N.Y.C. and WEST day-ahead on-peak highs in January 2025. The main loss is P5, the retail load obligation: it is short N.Y.C. and hedged only at WEST, and it grows with load. P2 gains only a little from the wider spread. P1 and P4 gain from higher WEST prices and gas and offset part of the loss. I estimate P5 loses about $10.9M and the long positions gain about $3M, for a net loss near $7.5M. I have not run the engine, so the figure is approximate and rests on scaling the supplied winter sensitivities.

A month-long cold snap combines a wide N.Y.C. premium with weak upstate prices. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $90/MWh for all 30 days, which hurts P5 and outweighs the small gain in P2. The peak load ratio is 1.06 and Henry Hub gas is up 40%. WEST on-peak is pushed 15% below what gas and load imply, as when upstate gas is cheaper than in the New York City pocket. That cut lowers the P1 and P4 gains. Real-time clears 30% above day-ahead, which costs P3, the off-peak day-ahead-minus-real-time position. A $8/MMBtu New York gas basis adds extra cost to the P4 heat-rate call. I estimate P5 loses about $11M plus load effects, and the other positions net to a gain of about $1.7M. The net loss is about $9M. This is an estimate scaled from the winter sensitivities, not an engine result.

A short, severe Elliott-style cold event lasts 10 days. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $250/MWh, below the 338.5 $/MWh real-time spread seen in Winter Storm Elliott, because forced outages and import curtailments leave the pocket short of supply. Peak load is 8% above a typical winter day (ratio 1.08) and Henry Hub gas is up 50%. WEST on-peak prices get no extra move. Real-time prices clear 50% above day-ahead, which costs P3 a little. P5 absorbs most of the loss, about $12M including load scaling. P1 and P4 gain about $1M from higher power prices and gas, and P3 loses a little. The net loss is about $9M. I have not run the engine, so this stated loss is approximate and rests on scaling the winter sensitivities.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A 30-day cold winter with mild gas stress and a persistent congested New York City pocket. Peak load runs 8% above a typical winter day (ratio 1.08), well inside the historical range. Henry Hub gas is up 20%, which is consistent with a cold snap. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $70/MWh for all 30 days because transfer limits keep upstate supply from reaching the city. WEST on-peak is pushed 20% below what gas and load imply, as when upstate is long supply. That trims the gains on the long P1 swap and the P4 heat-rate call. The main loss is P5, the retail load obligation: it is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price, hedged only at WEST, and its volume grows with load. P5 loses about $10M, and P2, P1 and P4 recover about $2M. The net loss is about $8M, with a stated figure of $7M. This is my scaling of the supplied winter sensitivities and the earlier engine results, not an engine run.

A 30-day cold period with only a slight load increase (ratio 1.03) and a small gas rise (Henry Hub +10%), kept small to stay close to ordinary winter conditions. The shock is a persistent $80/MWh widening of N.Y.C. minus WEST for all 30 days, from chronic New York City transmission and fuel constraints. WEST on-peak is cut a further 10% below what gas and load imply, which removes some of the long-power gains in P1 and P4. A $5/MMBtu New York gas basis is added to the P4 heat-rate call only. It cuts P4's payoff further without moving power prices. The loss comes mainly from P5, which is short N.Y.C. and hedged at WEST, so it loses about $10M or more over 30 days. P2 gains about $1.5M and P1 and P4 add a small gain. I estimate a net loss near $8M and state $7.5M. This is a hand estimate scaled from the supplied winter sensitivities, not an engine run.

A 14-day severe cold event with forced generator outages and constrained supply, as in Winter Storm Elliott where forced outages were about 1,800 MW. Peak load is 10% above a typical winter day (ratio 1.10) and Henry Hub gas is up 30%. N.Y.C. minus WEST widens by $150/MWh for 14 days because New York City is short of supply, and WEST on-peak is cut a further 25% below what gas and load imply. Real-time prices clear 40% above day-ahead, which costs P3, the off-peak day-ahead-minus-real-time position. It also lifts P1 somewhat. The main loss is P5, the retail load obligation, at about $10M or more because the spread shock is large, the volume is high and the WEST hedge loses value. P2 gains about $1.4M and P1, P4 and P3 net to a gain of about $1M. The net loss is about $8M, and I state $7M to be conservative. This is a hand estimate from the supplied sensitivities, not an engine run.

scenario.narrative: A severe multi-day heat wave lifts NYCA peak load to 1.20 times a typical summer day (load_peak_ratio 1.2, inside the 1.514 historical max) for 10 days. Air-conditioning load in N.Y.C. pushes the downstate import interfaces to their limits, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $180/MWh on top of the base spread (pocket_minus_ref_usd 180, below the 289.7 historical max). The book is hurt mainly through P5, the retail load obligation. It is short about 140 MW times the load ratio in N.Y.C. and hedged only at the WEST price, so it loses the full spread widening, scaled up by the extra load. The long spread in P2 offsets only about 15% of that loss. The higher load also lifts WEST prices, which helps P1 and P4 and partly cushions the loss. Rough estimate: P5 about -9.0M, P2 about +1.4M, load gains in P1 and P4 about +0.8M, net about -6.8M. Gas, real-time/day-ahead, WEST on-peak and spike shocks are set to zero because they would only help the long positions.

A prolonged, milder summer heat dome keeps NYCA peak load at 1.15 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.15) for 20 days. Persistent downstate transmission constraints and reduced N.Y.C. in-city generation margins keep the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread $90/MWh wider than normal (pocket_minus_ref_usd 90), well inside the historical range. The loss comes from the zone_volume channel. P5 is short N.Y.C. load at a fixed price and hedged at WEST, so every dollar of spread widening costs about 140 MW times 1.15 times 24 hours each day, for 20 days. P2, the long spread position, recovers only a small part of this. The extra load slightly raises WEST prices, giving P1 and P4 small gains, and it also increases P5's exposure. Rough estimate: P5 about -8.7M, P2 about +1.4M, load gains about +1.0M, extra load cost in P5 about -0.3M, net about -6.6M. This differs from scenario 1 by its longer duration and lower intensity, so the loss accumulates through persistence rather than severity. No price, gas or real-time/day-ahead shocks are applied.

During a 12-day heat wave, load is 1.20 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.2). Day-ahead markets over-schedule the heat and the realised load and prices come in below the day-ahead forecast. Real-time clears 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40, above the -84.1 historical minimum), which hurts the long WEST swap P1 and heat-rate call P4. Upstate WEST on-peak prices fall a further 30% on top of what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -30), because surplus upstate and import supply cannot reach N.Y.C. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $160/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 160, below the 289.7 historical max). Unlike scenarios 1 and 2, the loss combines the zone_volume channel with weak WEST prices and a day-ahead/real-time shock. Rough estimate: P5 about -9.6M, P2 about +1.5M, P1 and P4 losses from the WEST and real-time/day-ahead shocks about -1.1M, load gains about +0.9M, gains on P3 and P6 small, net about -8M, so I state a more conservative figure. Gas and spikes are zero because a spike would only help the long positions.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A month-long summer heat dome keeps NYCA peak load 8% above a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.08) for all 30 days. Sustained air-conditioning demand in N.Y.C. keeps the downstate interfaces tight, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread is $70/MWh wider on every day (pocket_minus_ref_usd 70). This is a persistent shock of about 2.4 standard deviations, not an extreme one-off spike. The loss is concentrated in P5, the retail load obligation: it is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and hedged only at WEST, so it pays the widening on 140 MW times the load ratio around the clock for 30 days. P2 is long the spread and recovers only about 15-20% of that loss. The higher load lifts WEST prices modestly and gives P1 and P4 small gains. Rough estimate: P5 about -9.0M, P2 about +1.6M, load gains about +0.9M, net about -6M. Gas, WEST on-peak, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero because they would only help the long positions. This is the lowest-intensity, longest-duration variant.

A 25-day heat wave with load only 5% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.05) hits N.Y.C. harder than upstate. Upstate WEST on-peak prices come in 20% weaker than the load shock alone implies (ref_onpeak_pct -20), because upstate generation is plentiful and cannot be exported to the city. That reduces the gains on the long WEST swap P1 and on the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $65/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 65) because of the same export limits and tight in-city margins. The loss comes from P5, which is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and hedged only at WEST, so it pays the full spread widening around the clock. P2 recovers a small part of that. Rough estimate: P5 about -7.0M, P2 about +1.2M, P1 and P4 losses from the weaker WEST price about -0.7M, load gains about +0.5M, net about -5.6M. Gas, real-time/day-ahead and spike shocks are zero. The mechanism is a congestion shock with a weak WEST price, not a pure load shock.

Over 30 days of a hot but well-forecast summer, load runs only 3% above normal (load_peak_ratio 1.03), which keeps the gains on P1 and P4 small. Upstate WEST on-peak prices are 25% below what load implies (ref_onpeak_pct -25) because upstate supply is ample. Real-time clears 30% below day-ahead (dart_pct -30) because day-ahead over-scheduled the heat. Both shocks cost the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, while P3 gains a little. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by only $45/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 45, about 1.6 standard deviations), the lowest spread shock of the three scenarios. The loss still comes mainly from P5, which pays this widening on 140 MW around the clock for 30 days. P2 recovers about 15%. Rough estimate: P5 about -5.7M, P2 about +1.0M, P1 and P4 losses from the WEST and real-time shocks about -2.2M, P3 about +0.2M, load gains about +0.2M, net about -6.5M. I state a lower figure because the effects are not additive. Gas and spike shocks are zero because they would only help the long positions. The mechanism combines weak upstate prices with a modest spread widening.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A hot but well-forecast 30-day summer spell in which load stays at a typical level (load_peak_ratio 1.0, the minimum allowed for a heat wave). The only physical stress is a modest N.Y.C. import constraint that widens the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread by $40/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 40, about 1.4 standard deviations). That is the smallest spread shock so far. P5 pays this widening on about 140 MW around the clock, and P2 recovers only part of it. WEST on-peak prices come in 35% below what the load and gas path implies (ref_onpeak_pct -35) because upstate supply is ample. Real-time clears 40% below day-ahead (dart_pct -40) because day-ahead over-scheduled the heat. Both shocks cut the value of the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4, while P3 gains slightly. Rough estimate: P5 about -4.1M, P2 about +0.7M, P1 and P4 about -3.0M, P3 about +0.3M, net about -6.1M. I state a lower figure because the effects are not additive. Gas and spike shocks are zero because they would only help the long positions.

A 20-day heat spell with typical peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) in which upstate is oversupplied and exports to N.Y.C. are constrained. WEST on-peak prices are 55% below what the load and gas path implies (ref_onpeak_pct -55, inside the -89.8 historical minimum). This is the main hit to the long WEST swap P1 and the heat-rate call P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $65/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 65) because of the same export limits. P5 pays that widening around the clock and P2 offsets only part of it. Real-time clears 10% below day-ahead (dart_pct -10), a small additional drag on P1 and P4, with a tiny gain on P3. This scenario differs from the earlier ones by relying on a deep WEST price drop over a medium duration, rather than on load or a large spread. Rough estimate: P5 about -4.5M, P2 about +0.8M, P1 and P4 about -1.85M, P3 about +0.1M, net about -5.5M. I state a lower figure because the effects are not additive. Gas and spike shocks are zero.

A 15-day heat wave lifts peak load to 1.10 times a typical day (load_peak_ratio 1.1), which raises P5's volume exposure in N.Y.C. In-city generation is tight and the import interfaces bind, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by $110/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd 110, about 3.8 standard deviations and well inside the 289.7 historical max). That is the main loss driver through P5. P2 offsets only part of it. Henry Hub is 20% lower (gas_hh_pct -20), a soft-gas backdrop that lowers WEST power and cuts the value of P1 and P4. WEST on-peak prices are a further 30% below what the load shock implies (ref_onpeak_pct -30) because upstate supply is ample. Real-time and day-ahead are left unchanged, and there are no spikes because they would only help the long positions. Rough estimate: P5 about -6.3M, P2 about +1.0M, P1 and P4 about -0.35M after the load gain offsets the weak prices, net about -5.7M. I state a lower figure because the effects are not additive.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: A pipeline constraint into the downstate region tightens delivered gas in the N.Y.C. area for 12 days. Henry Hub rises only 10 percent, so WEST power and the long WEST positions P1 and P4 gain little. The N.Y.C. gas basis jumps 20 $/MMBtu, which lowers the heat-rate call P4 payoff. Oil and dual-fuel units set the N.Y.C. price, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 150 $/MWh, well inside the historical winter range. The retail obligation P5 is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and loses roughly 3,300 $/MWh-day per $/MWh of widening on 3,360 MWh/day. The long spread P2 offsets only about 15 percent of that loss. Load is 4 percent above normal because of cold weather, which enlarges the P5 volume. Using the 5-day winter sensitivity, the net loss is about 3,880 $ per day per $/MWh of spread, or about 7.0M over 12 days. Small gains from P1 and P4 of about 0.1M reduce it to roughly 6.7M.

A month-long reduction in gas deliverability into the N.Y.C. area keeps downstate gas expensive for the full 30 days. Henry Hub rises 8 percent, which adds a small gain to P1 and P4. The N.Y.C. gas basis widens 12 $/MMBtu and lowers the heat-rate call P4 payoff. Downstate units burning costly gas or oil lift the N.Y.C. price relative to WEST, so the spread widens by a moderate 60 $/MWh for all 30 days. Load is 2 percent above normal. The retail load obligation P5 loses on every hour of the month, and the long spread P2 offsets only a small part. The 5-day winter sensitivity scales to about 3,880 $ per day per $/MWh of spread, so 60 $/MWh over 30 days is about 7.0M. Gas-driven gains on the long WEST positions of about 0.2M bring the net loss to roughly 6.5M. The shock is small but persistent, and it tests the book's exposure to duration rather than to a spike.

An acute gas supply failure hits the downstate region for 6 days, with a storm-like import and generator squeeze. Henry Hub rises 40 percent, which gives P1 and P4 only a modest gain. The N.Y.C. gas basis rises 30 $/MMBtu and cuts the P4 payoff. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 330 $/MWh, comparable to the N.Y.C. minus WEST real-time spread of 338.5 $/MWh in Winter Storm Elliott and below the 400.6 $/MWh historical winter maximum. Load stays at its normal level because the stress comes from supply. P5 is short N.Y.C. at a fixed price and takes most of the loss, and P2 offsets only a small part. The 5-day winter sensitivity gives about 3,880 $ per day per $/MWh of spread, so 330 $/MWh over 6 days is about 7.7M. Gains from higher WEST prices and gas of about 0.2M reduce the net loss to roughly 7.0M after allowing for nonlinearity.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.

1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).

7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Upstate pipeline export constraints trap gas in western New York for the full 30 days, while downstate gas stays tight. Cheap trapped gas pushes the WEST on-peak price down by 55 percent (ref_onpeak_pct = -55), with no Henry Hub move because the squeeze is regional. That fall hurts the long WEST swap P1, which loses when WEST drops toward and below K1, and it erodes the heat-rate call P4 payoff. Downstate oil and dual-fuel units set the N.Y.C. price, so the N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 40 $/MWh on every day. That is the main loss, in the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5, and the long spread P2 offsets only a small part. Rough scaling from the 5-day winter sensitivities gives P5 about -4.5M, P2 about +0.8M, P1 about -1.6M and P4 about -0.6M. The net is about -5.8M, and I am unsure how linear these scalings are over 30 days.

A 15-day downstate gas curtailment lifts the New York gas basis by 15 $/MMBtu above Henry Hub, which lowers the heat-rate call P4 payoff. Henry Hub rises only 5 percent (gas_hh_pct = 5), a mild national response. WEST power falls 30 percent on weak upstate demand and lower export value (ref_onpeak_pct = -30), so the long swap P1 loses against its 39.49 strike. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 90 $/MWh because costly gas and oil units set the N.Y.C. price, and that is the dominant loss in the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5. P2 offsets about 15 percent of the P5 loss. Scaled from the 5-day winter sensitivities, P5 is about -5.8M, P2 about +0.9M, P1 about -0.45M and P4 about -0.3M, for a net of roughly -5.5M. The estimate is uncertain because the scaling assumes linearity.

A 10-day gas supply squeeze hits downstate consumers during cold weather. Henry Hub rises 20 percent (gas_hh_pct = 20) and the New York gas basis rises 8 $/MMBtu, which cuts the P4 payoff. WEST on-peak power is hit by a further 40 percent decline (ref_onpeak_pct = -40) as upstate generation and imports are redirected, which weighs on P1 and P4. The N.Y.C. minus WEST spread widens by 140 $/MWh, which is inside the historical winter range, and the short N.Y.C. retail obligation P5 takes most of the loss. P2 offsets only a small part. Scaled from the 5-day winter sensitivities, P5 is about -6.2M, P2 about +0.95M, P1 about -0.4M less a small gas gain, and P4 about -0.3M, for a net of roughly -5.7M. This is a rough estimate with moderate uncertainty.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large loads upstate (data centers, fabs) arrive far slower than the Gold Book assumed, a 1500 MW shortfall (large_load_shock_mw -1500, load_peak_ratio 0.95) sustained for 30 days of summer. WEST demand is lower than expected, so the WEST on-peak price falls a further 25% (ref_onpeak_pct -25). That hurts the long P1 swap and the P4 heat-rate call. NYC load is unchanged and its import constraints stay binding, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $45/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +45). This is the dominant loss: the P5 retail short in NYC, hedged only with WEST, loses far more than P2 gains. Gas, dart, basis and spike shocks are zero. Estimate scales linearly from the 5-day sensitivities (spread net of P2 about 4.6M, WEST price and load about 1.6M), so it is approximate.

scenario.narrative: A 20-day summer episode in which the 2030-style large-load shortfall of about 900 MW materializes early (large_load_shock_mw -1000, load_peak_ratio 0.97). Weak WEST demand and soft gas (gas_hh_pct -20) push the WEST on-peak price down a further 45% (ref_onpeak_pct -45), so the long P1 swap and the P4 heat-rate call lose together. P4's loss is capped at its base payoff. NYC prices hold up, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $65/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +65). This hurts P5, whose WEST hedge is struck at 34.05 and falls in value while the NYC obligation is unchanged. P2 offsets only a small part. No spikes and no dart shock, because a dart increase would lift WEST prices and help P1. Estimate is linear scaling of the 5-day sensitivities, so it is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A shorter, sharper 15-day summer episode with a smaller near-term load miss of about 500 MW (large_load_shock_mw -500, load_peak_ratio 0.98). Congestion into NYC dominates: the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $90/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +90), inside the historical summer maximum, because upstate surplus cannot reach NYC while NYC supply stays tight. The widening hurts P5 much more than it helps P2. WEST on-peak is a further 30% lower (ref_onpeak_pct -30) on the slack upstate demand, hitting P1 and P4. A $1.00/MMBtu NY gas basis adds a small P4 loss (ny_gas_basis_usd 1.0). Gas, dart and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities (spread about 4.6M, WEST price and other effects about 0.7M), so the number is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

This is the main loss through P5 over every hour of the 30 days, and P2 recovers only a part. Dart, basis and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is a linear extrapolation of the 5-day sensitivities and the earlier engine results, so it is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A small large-load miss of about 300 MW (large_load_shock_mw -300) with normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) leaves upstate with excess energy for 30 days. WEST on-peak falls a further 35% (ref_onpeak_pct -35), which is the main loss on the long P1 swap and also hurts the P4 heat-rate call. NYC stays tight, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by a moderate $55/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +55). That is smaller than in the earlier scenarios and keeps the scenario nearer historical experience. P5 loses over the full 30 days and P2 offsets only a small part. A $1.00/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 1.0) lowers the P4 payoff slightly. No analogue fits a 300 MW miss, so confidence is low and the estimate is a linear extrapolation.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large-load connections slip by about 500 MW (large_load_shock_mw -500) while the daily peak stays at a normal summer level (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so NYC retail load keeps its full size. NYC import constraints stay tight for all 30 days, and the NYC minus WEST spread is $75/MWh wider than normal (pocket_minus_ref_usd +75). This is a pure zone-volume and congestion scenario. P5 is short 140 MW in NYC around the clock and its WEST hedge does not cover a wider spread. P2 earns back only 25 MW of that widening. The WEST on-peak price, gas, dart, basis and spike shocks are all zero, so P1 and P4 are not the loss driver. Estimate: P5 loses about 7.4M and P2 gains about 1.35M, a net of roughly 6M. It is based on the earlier engine results and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: The 2035-size large-load shortfall of about 1400 MW arrives early (large_load_shock_mw -1400) and lasts 30 days, while the daily peak is only slightly below normal (load_peak_ratio 0.99). Weak upstate demand coincides with a Henry Hub slump of 30% (gas_hh_pct -30), which cuts WEST power. WEST on-peak falls a further 15% (ref_onpeak_pct -15), so the long P1 swap and the P4 heat-rate call both lose. NYC stays supply-constrained, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $60/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +60). This hurts the P5 retail short for all 30 days, and P2 offsets only about 1.1M. Dart, basis and spike shocks are zero. Estimate: P5 about -6.0M, P1 about -1.0M, P4 about -0.4M, P2 about +1.1M. It is a linear extrapolation and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A large-load miss of about 1000 MW (large_load_shock_mw -1000) at normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) leaves upstate with a surplus for 30 days. The loss is shifted toward the system and gas channels. Gas is 25% lower (gas_hh_pct -25) and WEST on-peak falls a further 45% (ref_onpeak_pct -45). The long P1 swap, struck at 39.49, loses heavily, and the P4 heat-rate call loses its payoff. A $2.00/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2.0) cuts P4 slightly more. NYC stays tight, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by a smaller $50/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +50), which keeps the congestion shock closer to history. P5 still loses about 5M and P2 offsets about 0.9M. Dart and spike shocks are zero. Estimate: P1 about -1.8M, P4 about -0.8M. The total is uncertain.

CONSTRAINTS
- Hourly prices are clipped at a scenario cap of $5,000/MWh (a stated assumption of this exercise, not a NYISO rule); spike_daily_avg_usd is a daily on-peak average, so it also cannot exceed this.
- duration_days cannot exceed horizon_days; spike_days cannot exceed duration_days.
- spike_daily_avg_usd must be 0 when spike_days is 0 and positive otherwise.
- Shocks must be directionally consistent with the driver class (a cold snap raises load and gas, a heat wave raises load).
- Shock key mapping (agent key = internal key): ref_onpeak_pct = wh_onpeak_pct (WEST on-peak move), pocket_minus_ref_usd = dom_minus_wh_usd (N.Y.C. minus WEST, $/MWh), large_load_shock_mw = dc_load_shock_mw.
- Set stated_loss_usd to your own estimate of the book loss in USD (a number); it is compared with the engine's loss.
- Use numbers only (no ranges, no strings) for every shock. Use only the allowed enum values.
- If you cite an analogue, every claimed number must come from the analogue table and be within 30% of it. If no table entry fits, leave the analogue event empty and set confidence to low.

METHOD
1. State the causal chain from the physical driver to prices to the book's P&L.
2. Choose shock sizes that are extreme but plausible, and keep them mutually consistent.
3. Use different channels (system level, congestion, day-ahead vs real-time, gas, zone volume, tail) across your scenarios.
4. If the context has a 'book' table, read it with 'book_summary' and 'shock_glossary': pick shocks that hurt the positions that lose money (not shocks that only raise prices and gas, which make long positions gain), use 'shock_sensitivities' (if present) to see which shock moves which position and by how much, and stay inside 'shock_ceilings_by_season' (beyond implausible_above or below implausible_below a scenario is classed implausible).
5. Use the given driver family as driver_class and the given season as season in every scenario.
6. Signs must match the driver family (hard rule sign_consistent): for large_load_shortfall, large_load_shock_mw must be zero or negative and load_peak_ratio at most 1.0; for cold_snap and heat_wave, load_peak_ratio at least 1.0; for cold_snap and gas_supply, gas_hh_pct at least 0.
7. After each round you will receive engine numbers and rule verdicts only. Move shocks toward scenarios that breach the loss target with the smallest historical implausibility (small D^2, q at least 0.1%) and change direction when a rule fails.

scenario.narrative: Large-load connections slip by about 700 MW (large_load_shock_mw -700) while the daily peak stays at a normal summer level (load_peak_ratio 1.0), so NYC retail load keeps its full size for all 30 days. NYC import constraints stay tight and the NYC minus WEST spread is $58/MWh wider than normal (pocket_minus_ref_usd +58). P5 is short 140 MW in NYC around the clock and its WEST hedge does not cover the wider spread, which is the main loss. P2 earns back only 25 MW of the widening. Upstate surplus takes a further 25% off WEST on-peak (ref_onpeak_pct -25) and Henry Hub is 10% softer (gas_hh_pct -10), so P1 and P4 lose a little. Dart, basis and spike shocks are zero. The estimate is scaled from the earlier engine results (about $100k per $/MWh of spread for P5, $18k for P2) and is uncertain. No analogue fits a 700 MW miss.

The low end of the near-term large-load shortfall range, about 1500 MW (large_load_shock_mw -1500), hits at normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) and lasts 30 days. Upstate has a large energy surplus and Henry Hub is 30% lower (gas_hh_pct -30), so WEST on-peak falls a further 60% (ref_onpeak_pct -60), inside the historical summer minimum. The long P1 swap struck at 39.49 loses heavily, and the P4 heat-rate call loses most of its base payoff. A $2.00/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 2.0) adds a small further P4 loss. NYC stays tight, so the NYC minus WEST spread widens by only $40/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +40), so P5 loses about 4M and P2 offsets about 0.7M. Dart and spike shocks are zero. This puts the loss mainly in the system and gas channels. The estimate is a scaled extrapolation of the earlier engine results and is uncertain.

scenario.narrative: A 2030-style large-load shortfall of about 900 MW (large_load_shock_mw -900) at normal peak load (load_peak_ratio 1.0) lasts 24 days. NYC stays supply-constrained and the NYC minus WEST spread widens by $68/MWh (pocket_minus_ref_usd +68), the main loss through the P5 retail short, with P2 offsetting part of it. Weak upstate demand lowers Henry Hub by 20% (gas_hh_pct -20) and takes a further 30% off WEST on-peak (ref_onpeak_pct -30), so the long P1 swap loses. A $1.50/MMBtu NY gas basis (ny_gas_basis_usd 1.5) trims the P4 payoff. Dart and spike shocks are zero. The shorter 24-day duration scales the 30-day losses by about 0.8. Estimate: P5 about -5.5M, P2 about +1.0M, P1 about -1.0M, P4 about -0.5M. The total is uncertain.
